Dear Hiring Manager,

After ten years at Nordkom Radar Systems I know ground-surveillance signal processing fairly well, and I have enough self-awareness to recognise that I have absorbed most of what this particular product line can teach me. Your posting caught my attention because Kaikuvaara's problems sound harder and more interesting — tighter link budgets, wider instantaneous bandwidths, arrays that need to perform at the edge of what the physics will actually allow. That is the kind of work I want to spend the next stage of my career on.

My route into radar was slightly unusual. During my final year at Tampere I did a six-month placement with a local Tier-1 automotive supplier, writing engine-control-unit embedded software in C — real-time injection-timing routines and sensor-readout loops running on Infineon TriCore hardware, strict SafeC compliance, nightly regression on the hardware-in-the-loop bench. It was not radar, but it was hard real-time on deeply constrained hardware, and it gave me habits around cycle budgets and fixed-point arithmetic that I still rely on. When I joined Nordkom in 2016, that foundation turned out to matter more than I had expected: the discipline that keeps an ECU stable at 40 kHz is the same discipline that keeps a range-gating pipeline from dropping samples on a loaded processor.

At Nordkom I moved into phased-array beamforming, built up the Python data-processing infrastructure that runs our field-trial pipeline, led a small waveform-design team through a product refresh, and spent more hours in the near-field range than I can count. It has been a good decade and I am grateful for it. But the SV product family is mature now. Most of the work has shifted to integration and sustaining engineering, and I find myself spending evenings reading about new array architectures with a kind of restlessness that tells me it is time for a change.

I am based in Oulu already, so no relocation is involved. Happy to discuss further.

Nils Kovac
